title: Release Plan
description: The release plan that survives contact with stakeholders — versus the Gantt chart that looks impressive in a meeting and crumbles by week three. Four sections, written in commitments not aspirations. The discipline is being honest about what we commit to versus what we hope to deliver.

# [Product / programme] — Release Plan
_For [release window] · v[N] · last updated [date]_

## 1. The release in one paragraph
_What is shipping. Who it's for. Why this release, not the next one._

## 2. Committed scope
_The features we are committing to ship in this release window. Each one: title, sized estimate, the user outcome it serves. Sized commitments only — anything un-sized goes in section 3._

## 3. Stretch scope
_Features we will deliver if committed scope lands ahead of schedule. NEVER blurred into committed scope. Explicitly conditional._

## 4. Out of release
_What is NOT in this release that someone might assume is. Explicit list. This section prevents the 'I thought you were doing X' conversation._

## 5. Key dates + dependencies
_Hard dates (external commitments, regulator deadlines). Soft dates (internal commitments). Dependencies with named owners._

## 6. The one thing that could derail this
_Name it. Specifically. Not 'team availability'; 'Lewis's parental leave overlaps with the integration testing window'._

# Customer Portal v1 — Release Plan
_For go-live 9 September 2026 · v0.4 · 28 April 2026_

## 1. The release in one paragraph

Replace the legacy customer portal for top-12 B2B customers. Go-live 9 September; CS hard-cutover begins the same day. Self-service experience covering: account management, three report types, password reset, admin console. Sized to 16 weeks of programme work; we are in week 10.

## 2. Committed scope

| Feature | Size | User outcome |
|---------|------|--------------|
| Login + account view | 8 pts | Top-12 admin can log in and see their org's user list |
| User management (add / remove / role-change) | 13 pts | Top-12 admin can manage their own user list without raising a ticket |
| Three report types (usage, billing, audit) | 13 pts | Top-12 admin can see their org's standard reports without contacting CS |
| Self-service password reset | 5 pts | Top-12 portal users can reset their password without raising a ticket |
| Admin console (CS-side audit log + impersonation) | 8 pts | CS team can audit customer-admin actions and impersonate for support cases |

## 3. Stretch scope

- **Bulk-import upload v1** (8 pts est., not refined). Will deliver if committed scope lands by week 14. Otherwise Q4.
- **Custom-period date range on reports** (3 pts). Will deliver if committed scope lands by week 15.

## 4. Out of release

- Historical data migration for accounts >24 months old (Phase 2; declined at programme charter).
- Mobile-responsive admin console (Phase 2; CS confirmed acceptable to wait until Q4).
- API for customer-data export (Q4 candidate; Tobi notified).
- White-label theming (Q3 candidate; Bilqis aware).
- Real-time chat support (declined week 6; Folake withdrew the ask).

## 5. Key dates + dependencies

| Date | Type | Dependency | Owner | Status |
|------|------|------------|-------|--------|
| 14 June | Hard | SSO config from IT | Tomasz Wójcik | On track |
| 28 June | Hard | Customer-data pipeline (data platform team) | Rohan Chatterjee | At risk — see RAID R-04 |
| 8 August | Hard | Compliance data-residency sign-off | Marcus Klein | Open — meeting week 7 |
| 18 August | Soft | UAT cycle starts (top-12 end-user pool ≥24) | Janelle Ofori | At risk — currently 17 of 24 |
| 1 September | Soft | CS hard-cutover policy ratified | CS Director | Confirmed week 4 |
| 9 September | Hard | Go-live cutover | [PO + PM] | — |

## 6. The one thing that could derail this

The customer-data pipeline from the data platform team (R-04). It's tracked, escalated, mitigated — but if it slips beyond mid-July, UAT can't start on time, which collapses the cutover window. Everything else has float; this one doesn't. Watching weekly with Rohan.

annotations.note: One paragraph, plain English. The release in five sentences. If you can't compress it to this, the team can't either, and stakeholders won't remember what's in it.

Stretch scope NEVER blurred into committed scope. The first time a stretch item drifts into commit territory without re-planning, the team has lost the discipline. Make it explicit: 'will deliver if X lands by Y'.

Out-of-release section is the most valuable single section in the document. Six weeks in, someone will say 'I thought you were doing white-label theming for this release'. With this section, the answer is 'no, here's where we documented that'. Without it, the conversation becomes a fresh argument.

The 'one thing that could derail this' section forces honesty. If you can't name the single highest-risk thing, you haven't been paying attention. Naming it doesn't make it worse; it makes the mitigation conversation real.

common_mistakes: Committed scope inflated. The PO commits to everything because saying no in section 2 is harder than saying no in section 4. Resist; the release won't ship if section 2 is a wishlist.
Stretch scope omitted. Without it, the team has nothing to pull from when committed scope lands ahead of schedule, and ends up either coasting or asking the PO mid-release.
Out-of-release section omitted because 'obvious'. Never obvious. Always populate.
Key dates without owners. 'IT' is not an owner. Name the human.
'The one thing that could derail this' written generically ('team capacity'). Specific. Name the actual risk.
Release plan written once and never updated. By week 6 the plan is stale; stakeholders are working from outdated information. Revise weekly at first, monthly once the plan is stable.
variant_patterns: Multi-release variant (annual roadmap): each release gets its own plan; the roadmap references each. Don't try to make a single document do both jobs.
Regulatory release variant: add §0 'Regulatory commitment' — what the regulator requires by which date. Section 5 dates almost always run through the regulator's calendar.

Trial / beta release variant: section 2 becomes 'features in the beta'; section 4 becomes 'features deliberately NOT in beta (and why we're holding them back)'. The discipline is being honest about what beta is for.
